searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Nine were restricted to a house's own domain and are read as primary through their summaries: paternosterwine.it twice (the history; the Don Anselmo page and the Barone Rotondo pages), elenafuccivini.com twice (the Titolo pages, the wine club sheets), cantinedelnotaio.it once (La Firma and the house's list), librandi.it twice (Tenuta Ponta and Duca Sanfelice; Gravello) and ceratti.it with agriturismoceratti.com twice (the house; the light label). Most of the rest blocked the author's own sources (WineNews, Gambero Rosso International, Corriere del Vino, AIS, Falstaff, Superiore.de, DoctorWine, Decanter, the Wine Scholar Guild, the VITIS host and Wein-plus) so that an independent account would show. The Cirò rules searches are counted with Librandi and serve the Ceratti question too. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept in a record marked checked.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the houses' own pages and sheets for their own dates and methods and to the appellation texts, then to the press and the merchants, with the author's sources blocked where they would only have repeated themselves.

Where the sources corrected the record (Rotondo replaced by Barone Rotondo, Titolo's year in barrique, La Firma's Superiore bottlings, Gravello's first vintage and its IGT, the Cirò Classico DOCG's rules, Ceratti's village, bottlings and making, the vine of Greco di Bianco) it was set right with its source; where a claim rested on one source among those read (the first DOC of the province of Reggio Calabria, the twenty four months of one page's heading, Il Rogito) it was cut.
A writer's own blog, met in several results, was read for orientation only and is cited nowhere; prices, scores, guide awards, hectares and bottle counts were read and not used.

tested: The founding of 1925 and the founder's first bottles: the house's own history page (read through search) dates the first bottles of the founder's Aglianico to 1925 and gives his birth as 1898; Slowine's centenary piece and Travel Eat agree on 1925. Confirmed; the founder stays described, since no source read gives the year of his death.

The first Don Anselmo of 1985: Travel Eat (the wine created in 1985 in the founder's honour) and Vinup (the 1985 vintage, the move from chestnut to Slavonian oak) bear out WineNews and Gambero Rosso; one search summary had the house's page put the Don Anselmo label on the bottles of 1925, which no other source says and which reads as a loose summary. Confirmed as 1985.

The site and the making: the house's Don Anselmo page gives Gelosia at Barile at 600 metres, fifteen to eighteen days on the skins in steel with pumping over and délestage, then about two years in wood, half in large Slavonian oak casks and half in French barriques used once, and a year in bottle. Confirmed by the primary; the 2015 sheet's other cellar stays in open.

The rules: Agraria.org, the Basilicata Chamber of Commerce and Italian Wine Central give the DOC by the decree of 18 February 1971 and the Superiore DOCG by the ministerial decree of 2 August 2010, with three years of ageing including twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle, and five years for the Riserva. Confirmed: the label term, the classification, the trap and the wine question stand.

The Tommasi majority of 2016: Tommasi Family Estates' own notice, Turismo del Gusto and Slowine give a majority taken in mid August 2016, the share kept private and the family staying in the running of the house. Confirmed.

Rotondo: the house's own pages (Barone Rotondo, a new chapter) say Barone Rotondo takes the place of Rotondo, which was born in the 1990s; Vinous lists a Rotondo of 2011 and the first Barone Rotondo is the 2020 vintage. The record said Rotondo joined later and stood as the house's other wine; set right.

The house rules: nobody living named (the winemaker quoted, the fourth generation's oenologist and the Tommasi family's members, met in results, are not named; the Tommasi family is named as a house); no price, no score (scores met in results are not used); no volatile size (the twenty hectares met are not used); British; no dash. The questions: one key each, the distractors of one kind (four promises of a label word; four families of Italian houses), the explanations teach the Riserva and Taurasi.

changed.was: Paternoster dates itself to 1925, when the founder began to sell his Aglianico in bottles under the family's name at Barile, a village on the slopes of Monte Vulture whose cellars are cut into the soft volcanic tuff. For decades the house made the dark, firm, long aged Aglianico of the old Vulture school. Aglianico del Vulture became a DOC in 1971, and in 1985 the family made the first Don Anselmo, named in the founder's honour and drawn from old vines on the hills around Barile, Gelosia among them. It became the house's flagship, given about two years in wood and a year in bottle before it leaves the cellar. A single vineyard red, Rotondo, joined it later in a more modern style. In 2010 the zone's longer aged wine was raised to the Aglianico del Vulture Superiore DOCG, and the house's later sheets print Superiore on Don Anselmo. In August 2016 the Tommasi family of Valpolicella took a majority of the house, and in 2025 Paternoster marked its century with tastings of old vintages of Don Anselmo. To a sommelier it is the long standing reference of the Vulture: Aglianico from volcanic slopes, built to be kept.

tested: The story: Città del Vino and the Movimento Turismo del Vino tell it as the house does: the grandfather bought the highest part of Contrada Solagna del Titolo in the 1960s; the family weighed a sale around 2000 and the founder, then a student of viticulture and oenology, kept the vines, among the oldest on the Vulture by her account; the estate began with the 2000 vintage with an outside consultant and from 2004 was run by her; from the start one wine, Titolo. Confirmed; the near sale now hedged as the house's account.

The site: K&L's note from Decanter gives about 600 metres on the highest part of the Vulture zone, a vineyard named for the Solagna del Titolo district, on compressed volcanic ash, tuff and pumice; no source but the house speaks of clay. The height and the highest part stand on the house and two others; the clay is now hedged as the house's account.

The making: the house's wine club sheets (2017, 2018) give the malolactic in barriques of two hundred litres, half new, for twelve months in all, and twelve months in bottle; the Titolo Classico page gives twenty four months in its heading but the same twelve in its own text, and twenty four months is the figure of the house's Titolo Superiore page; Decanter, through K&L, gives twelve months in first and second use barriques. So about a year in barrique, and the record's 'two on the house's newest page' is cut.

The appellation: the Titolo Classico page's heading says DOC while its field of denomination reads DOCG Superiore; the house's separate Titolo Superiore (Superiore DOCG, twenty four months in barriques) and Titolo Riserva (Superiore Riserva DOCG, a year in barriques and two in new tonneaux of five hundred litres) and Zachys's listing of the Riserva show the classic Titolo is the DOC wine, with Falstaff's DOC. Confirmed as the DOC, with classification empty.

The house rules: the founder is named only in the house's name; her grandfather and great grandfather, met by name in results, are not named; the vineyard's size and the vines' ages in years are not used; no price, no score; British; no dash. The questions: one key each, the distractors of one kind (four readings of a label word; four events of a founding), the explanations teach.

changed.was: The vineyards behind this estate were bought in the 1960s by the founder's grandfather, who chose the highest part of Contrada Solagna del Titolo at Barile, at the foot of the extinct volcano of Monte Vulture. By 2000 the family meant to sell them: the vines were too much to keep for pleasure, and the children were expected to leave home for university. At the last moment the founder, then a student of viticulture and oenology, could not accept that the vineyard she had grown up in, holding by the house's account some of the oldest vines on the Vulture, would pass to another name. The family kept the land, the estate began with the 2000 vintage, and from the first it put everything into a single wine named for the vineyard, Titolo. An outside consultant helped at first; from 2004 the founder ran every part of the estate herself, in the vineyard and in the cellar. Titolo ages in French barriques and then in bottle, and the house has since added a Riserva from the same vineyard. To a sommelier it is a lesson in what one high, old vineyard on Vulture's volcanic ash and clay can give to Aglianico, and a reminder that a young estate can carry an old vineyard's name.

changed.was: Cantine del Notaio was founded in 1998 at Rionero in Vulture by a graduate in agricultural science and his wife, to make Aglianico del Vulture from the family's own vineyards. By the house's account the family had worked vines on the Vulture for seven generations, and the founder's grandfather, whose name he shared, left those vineyards to him. The house's name, the notary's cellars, honours the notary of the family, the founder's father, who began work as a notary at Rionero in 1959, and its wines take their names from a notary's office: Il Preliminare, Il Repertorio, Il Sigillo, Il Rogito and La Firma, the signature at the foot of a deed. The house brought back into use its own caves in the centre of Rionero, cut into the volcanic tuff in the seventeenth century, by its account, and used by Franciscan friars; they hold the barriques in which La Firma ages. La Firma comes from Aglianico picked in the first days of November, aged a year in new French oak and a year in bottle. To a sommelier it shows the Vulture in a riper, oak framed style beside the long aged Aglianico of neighbouring Barile, and why the zone digs its cellars rather than building them.

changed.was: Librandi traces its roots to the vineyard at Ponta that the founder planted in the 1950s, by the house's account, and in 1953 the family began to bottle wine in a small cellar on Via Tirone at Cirò Marina. Cirò became a DOC in 1969. The founder's two sons built the house together for some forty years, one at the making and selling of the wines, the other at the cellar, the staff and the accounts, and in 1975 they opened a new winery in Contrada San Gennaro on the coast road at Cirò Marina. In 1988 the house released its first Gravello, which joins Gaglioppo to Cabernet Sauvignon and which it calls its flagship. From 1993 the family planted experimental vineyards to save Calabria's forgotten grapes, Magliocco and Mantonico among them. The brothers led the house until 2012, when the next generation took charge, and in 2025 Cirò Classico became Calabria's first DOCG. Duca Sanfelice, pure Gaglioppo from the founder's vines aged in steel rather than wood, is the house's Cirò in its classic form, and the bottle a sommelier reaches for to teach the appellation.

The making: the house lays the bunches on racks in the sun, destems and presses them gently and bottles after about two years; it gives a loss of weight of up to half, where the DOC's text (Disciplinare.it, the national register) allows drying in the sun on cane mats or in forced air rooms with a loss of up to 35 per cent. The DOC: Wikipedia and Lavinium give the decree of 18 June 1980 (Gazzetta Ufficiale of 12 December 1980) and the zone of Bianco and part of Casignana; the passito the only type by the rules. The serve: the house advises 10 to 12 degrees Celsius on one page and 6 to 8 to 10 to 12 by use on another; the record keeps the Codex's 6 to 8 for a sweet white and gives the house's warmer range. The drinking window now carries the house's two or three years after the harvest.

The grape of this wine was long known as Greco di Gerace, after the old town of the same coast. On 18 June 1980 a decree made Greco di Bianco a DOC, the first of the province of Reggio Calabria, and its rules allow a single wine: a passito of at least ninety five per cent Greco Bianco from Bianco and part of neighbouring Casignana, the vintage on every label and no Superiore or Riserva. In 2006 a DNA study found that Greco di Gerace shares its genetic profile with Malvasia delle Lipari and Malvasia di Sardegna, and with Malvasias of Spain and Croatia, so the vine is an old variety met across the Mediterranean under other names. Ceratti is a family estate of the zone, known for this one wine, which it bottles under a white label and a black. To a sommelier the wine is a rare taste of the sweet tradition of Calabria's toe, and a lesson that a name such as Greco can mislead.

swaps.proposed: The author kept the plan's Duca Sanfelice and put to the checker either keeping it, saying plainly that the house calls Gravello its flagship, or a swap to Gravello under a new key, since the house's own Gravello page calls Gravello the flagship wine of the company.
swaps.why: The house's own Gravello page does call Gravello its flagship, and the record already says so three times: in others, in a trap and in the story question, so a learner meets the house's flagship by name. But the group exists to teach Calabria and Basilicata, and the region record names Cirò, Gaglioppo on the Ionian coast, as Calabria's signature red; Duca Sanfelice is the house's Cirò Rosso Classico Superiore Riserva of Gaglioppo alone from its oldest alberello vines at Ponta, the estate where its research on the native vines began in 1993, by the house's own pages, which speak of it as the house's leading Gaglioppo. Gravello is a Gaglioppo and Cabernet Sauvignon blend labelled outside the appellation, Val di Neto IGT and later Calabria IGT; a swap would leave the group without a Cirò while the region record teaches Cirò and its new DOCG. The plan's note chose Duca Sanfelice for this reason, and the record's every fact now stands on the house's sheet and two independent accounts. As in the Lanzerac and Louis Magnin rulings, the pick is kept and the record tells the truth about it; nothing is to be changed in plan.json, and the integrator may revisit if the owner reads flagship as the house's word alone.
